EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  
“Economic Legacies of the American Dust Bowl”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) complemented with an event-study (dynamic DID).

Rationale  
• The Dust Bowl was a large, temporally concentrated environmental shock that hit some counties much harder than others.  
• We observe repeated county-level outcomes (1920-1970) both before and after the shock.  
• DID exploits cross-sectional variation in exogenous exposure (treated vs. comparison counties) and time variation (pre- vs. post-shock).  
• The event-study extension lets us trace short-run (1930s) and long-run (1940-1970) adjustment paths.  
• A continuous-intensity DID (using a standardized “dust‐severity index”) improves efficiency and avoids arbitrary treatment cut-offs, yet still rests on the same identifying assumptions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• DustSeverityc ≡ standardized z-score of cumulative dust storm days 1930–1936 / acres cropland eroded / average Palmer Drought Severity Index, constructed from U.S. Weather Bureau and Soil Conservation Service archives.  
• Baseline binary: Treatedc = 1{DustSeverityc ≥ 75th percentile among Plains counties}. Robustness: continuous specification.

Control group  
• Counties in the same nine Plains states whose DustSeverity is below the 25th percentile (“low-exposure” Plains counties).  
• Using only Plains states keeps pre-1930 agricultural structure, rainfall levels, and New Deal policy exposure comparable.

Treatment timing  
• t = 1934 chosen as the canonical “shock year” (peak storms).  
• Pre-period: 1920, 1925, 1930 censuses.  
• Post-period: 1940, 1950, 1960, 1970 censuses.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends: In the absence of the Dust Bowl, high- and low-exposure counties would have had similar outcome trends.  
   • Plausibility: 1920-1930 trends in wheat yield, population, and land values can be inspected; mechanised agriculture and rail access spread fairly uniformly across the Plains in the 1920s.

A2. No Anticipation: Farmers did not foresee the unprecedented scale of dust storms before 1930 and therefore did not adjust land use pre-emptively.  
   • Plausibility: Contemporary agronomists misdiagnosed the problem; severe storms only began winter 1932–33.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): A county’s outcomes respond only to its own exposure, not to neighbouring counties’ exposure (no spillovers).  
   • Plausibility: Some migration spillovers exist; we will test spillovers explicitly (see Threat #2).

A4. Composition Stability: Census re-definitions of county boundaries are minimal; population measures refer to the same geographic units over time.  
   • Plausibility: Fewer than 2 % of continental U.S. counties changed boundaries after 1920; shapefiles confirm stability for study area.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Great Depression confounding (nation-wide shock).  
   • Difference-in-differences already nets out common macro shocks by year fixed effects.  
   • Additional mitigation: control for county-level agricultural price indices interacted with pre-1930 crop mix; include state-specific linear trends.

T2. Out-migration spillovers and “contagion” into control counties.  
   • Strategy:  
     a) Construct adjacency matrix; drop “ring” of counties that border treated counties (leave-one-ring-out).  
     b) Estimate spatial HAC (Conley) standard errors.  
     c) Run placebo DID on neighbouring counties only (should be zero if spillovers limited).

T3. Heterogeneous New Deal aid (AAA, Soil Conservation Service) targeted to hardest-hit counties.  
   • Collect county-level AAA payment data 1933–40; include as control or interact with time dummies.  
   • Instrumental-variables robustness: instrument DustSeverity with ex-ante exogenous soil erodibility (texture, slope) interacted with drought intensity—policy makers could not manipulate pre-existing soil.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)     # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)         # TWFE & Sun-Abraham event studies
library(ggplot2)
library(conleyreg)      # spatial SEs

# 1. Load Data
ag   <- fread("county_ag_census_1920_1970.csv")   # yields, land values
pop  <- fread("county_population_census_1920_1970.csv")
wx   <- fread("dust_severity_index.csv")          # constructed external file

# 2. Merge & Construct Variables
df <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y,by = c("fips","year"), all=TRUE),
             list(ag, pop, wx))

# Treatment variables
p75 <- quantile(df$DustSeverity_1930s, .75, na.rm = TRUE)
p25 <- quantile(df$DustSeverity_1930s, .25, na.rm = TRUE)
df[, treated := as.integer(DustSeverity_1930s >= p75)]
df[, control_plains := as.integer(DustSeverity_1930s <= p25)]

# Keep treated and control counties only
df <- df[treated==1 | control_plains==1]

# Time variables
df[, post := as.integer(year >= 1934)]

# Outcomes
df[, ln_yield := log(wheat_bushels_per_acre)]
df[, ln_pop   := log(total_population)]
df[, ln_land  := log(real_land_value)]

# 3. Main DID (short-run 1940 outcome example)
did_ag <- feols(ln_yield ~ treated*post | fips + year,
                data = df[year %in% c(1930, 1940)],
                cluster = "fips")
summary(did_ag)

# 4. Dynamic Event-Study (1920-1970)
es <- feols(ln_yield ~ sunab(treated_year, year) | fips + year,
            data = df[, treated_year := ifelse(treated==1, 1934, 0)],
            weights = pop_1930,  cluster = "fips")
iplot(es) + ggtitle("Event-study: Wheat yield")

# 5. Robustness: Leave-one-ring-out
border <- fread("county_borders.csv")  # adjacency list (fips_i, fips_j, border=1)
ring1  <- border[fips_i %in% df[treated==1, fips], unique(fips_j)]
df_lo  <- df[!fips %in% ring1]
did_lo <- feols(ln_yield ~ treated*post | fips + year,
                data = df_lo[year %in% c(1930, 1940)],
                cluster = "fips")
etable(did_ag, did_lo)

# Conley SEs for spatial correlation
conley  <- conleyreg(did_ag, lat="lat", lon="lon", radius=100) # 100 km radius
conley
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Direction: Negative short-run effects on agricultural productivity (≥ −15 % wheat yield), land values (≥ −25 %) and county population (out-migration of 5–10 %).  
Long-run: Partial recovery in yields (gap shrinks to −5 % by 1970) but persistent population loss (still −8 % vs. counterfactual) reflecting lasting demographic reallocation.

Economic intuition: Soil erosion and capital loss depress productivity quickly; over decades, soil conservation and technological change close part of the gap, but human capital reallocates permanently.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Pre-trends visually flat and statistically insignificant  (1)  
C2: No anticipation documented in historical agronomy reports (1)  
C3: Composition (county boundaries, measurement) stable        (1)  
C4: No major spillovers or they are controlled/tested          (0.5)  
C5: Treatment not correlated with other policy shocks          (0.5)  

Total = 4/5  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
End of plan
